notes: Section 423 transaction-at-undervalue claim with trust and charging order issues; outcome and statutory purpose analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Setting aside property transfers to defeat service charge judgments
key_facts: Beckenham MC Ltd obtained county court judgments for unpaid service charges against Centralex Ltd and Karlton London Ltd in respect of two business units at Metro Business Centre.
During and after the proceedings Centralex and Karlton London transferred Units 29 and 30 for no consideration through related companies to Congress and Mortimer.
The respondents claimed the units were held on trust for Pasonic International Corporation and that trust terms excluded the trustee's right of indemnity for service charges.
Dr Tayfoor admitted the later transfers were intended to keep the beneficial owner's property free of the defendants' debts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 423 of the Insolvency Act 1986 to set aside transfers and for charging orders, following an interim injunction restraining sale.
enrichment.outcome: Applicant held entitled in principle to section 423 relief; form of order deferred pending possible restoration of dissolved Centralex to the register.
enrichment.ratio: A transfer of bare legal title for no consideration is a transaction at an undervalue under section 423(1)(a); where a county court judgment for service charges was incurred by a trustee qua proprietor enjoying concomitant land rights, it is a liability incurred on behalf of the trust so that section 2(1)(b)(i) of the Charging Orders Act 1979 applies; transfers substantially motivated to put assets beyond reach of a creditor satisfy section 423(3).
legal_issues: Whether transfers for no consideration were transactions at an undervalue
Whether the applicant was a victim prejudiced by the transactions
Effect of an alleged trust excluding trustee indemnity
Whether judgments were obtained against trustees within section 2(1)(b)(i) of the Charging Orders Act 1979
Whether the statutory purpose in section 423(3) was established

confidence.notes: Core insolvency and charging order reasoning is explicit. Final orders were deferred pending company restoration.

notes: Section 288 planning challenge; tree preservation reasoning quashed and noise ground linked; inspector decision analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Planning appeal quashed over tree preservation and noise reasoning
key_facts: The Qaadria Jilaani Trust applied to convert domestic premises at 5 Millfields Road, Wellington into a community training centre for the local Muslim community.
Telford and Wrekin Council refused permission on residential amenity and tree preservation grounds.
An Inspector dismissed the appeal, relying on Policy EH4 on noise from traffic and Policy OL11 on protected trees.
The claimants' arboricultural expert proposed a no-dig construction method, but the Council adduced no contrary evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against an Inspector's refusal of planning permission on appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; the Inspector's decision quashed because the tree preservation reasoning was unintelligible and could not be disassociated from the noise ground.
enrichment.ratio: Where the only expert evidence supports a no-dig method preserving protected trees but the Inspector reasons from digging-based experience and a 4-metre construction width rule without explaining rejection of the expert's method, the decision is unintelligible; when one refusal ground fails and the grounds are not truly independent, the whole decision cannot stand.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector's tree preservation reasoning was adequate
Whether Policy EH4 was properly applied to noise from vehicular and pedestrian traffic
Whether the noise and tree grounds were independent
Whether personal permission under Circular 11/95 paragraph 93 was appropriate
Whether a temporary trial permission should have been considered

confidence.notes: Outcome and principal legal errors are clear. Permission to appeal was refused as fact-specific.

notes: Share purchase indemnity and contractual time bar construction; ICS v West Bromwich principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Pension under-funding indemnity construction in share purchase agreement
key_facts: Snowville UK Ltd bought Baldwin PLC from Holidaybreak Plc under an agreement containing an indemnity for under-funding of Mr Singh's Baldwin pension.
Mr Singh claimed Baldwin owed £688,000 to the pension scheme following an actuary's letter; no payment was made and Baldwin later entered administrative receivership.
Master Price held the indemnity covered liability but that clause 4.6.4 time limits barred the claim.
The scheme rules allowed Baldwin to stop contributing if further contributions were impracticable or inexpedient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a strike-out/summary judgment order on construction of a share purchase indemnity and contractual notification time limits.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on time limits; cross-appeal dismissed on indemnity construction; claim reinstated subject to reframing.
enrichment.ratio: Where background shows parties intended a meaningful pension under-funding indemnity, the court may construe defective drafting under ICS v West Bromwich principles to indemnify Baldwin against Mr Singh's service agreement claims relating to scheme under-funding; clause 4.8.1's 'without prejudice to clause 4.6.4' preserves separate operation of the clauses and does not incorporate the clause 4.6.4 time bar into the indemnity.
legal_issues: Whether the indemnity covered any real liability or was meaningless on its face
Whether claims by Mr Singh under his service agreement fell within 'payable pursuant to the Pension Scheme'
Whether Baldwin remained liable to scheme trustees despite discretionary cessation of contributions
Whether clause 4.6.4 time limits applied to indemnity claims through clause 4.8
linked_authorities: ICS Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
Co-operative Wholesale Society Ltd v National Westminster Bank plc [1995] 1 EGLR 97

confidence.notes: Construction and time limit issues are fully reasoned. Claim framing concerns noted but do not affect enrichment.

notes: Barrister negligence permission application; Lucas direction and tactical decision analysis is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Barrister negligence claim over Lucas alibi direction refusal
key_facts: Popat was convicted at the Old Bailey of attempted rape and related offences but later acquitted after CCRC referral and retrial.
He sued trial and appeal counsel for failing to raise the judge's omission of the Lucas limb of the alibi direction.
Buckley J held counsel deliberately chose not to raise the point at trial or on first appeal for tactical reasons and was not clearly wrong.
The second Court of Appeal quashed the conviction on multiple summing-up grounds, of which the Lucas point was only one.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against dismissal of a barrister negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no basis to interfere with Buckley J's finding that counsel was not negligent.
enrichment.ratio: Counsel may justifiably refrain from inviting correction of an incomplete alibi direction at trial where doing so could disadvantage the client, and a deliberate tactical trial decision does not necessarily require raising the same point on appeal; failure to do so is not negligent where contemporaneous authority discouraged appealing deliberate trial decisions and the omitted direction was not critical to the later successful appeal.
legal_issues: Whether counsel breached duty by not correcting the Lucas alibi direction at trial
Whether counsel was negligent for omitting the point from the first criminal appeal
Whether the omitted direction caused loss
Effect of counsel's £250,000 insurance limit remark

confidence.notes: Permission decision and negligence reasoning are clear. Quantum appeal not decided.

notes: Costs-only decision after ECJ milk levy reference; narrow procedural issue clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Costs after failed milk levy claim and ECJ Article 10 lifeline
key_facts: Penycoed Farming Partnership claimed milk levy from the Intervention Board for Agricultural Produce for excess production.
Master Eyre refused to strike out the claim; the Court of Appeal referred questions to the ECJ.
The ECJ held Articles 1 and 2 of Regulation 3950/92 did not permit direct recovery but suggested a possible Article 10 route.
The claimants sought leave to amend on the Article 10 basis; the defendants did not oppose amendment but sought costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on costs following an ECJ reference on whether direct levy recovery was permitted under Regulation 3950/92.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; defendants awarded costs of the strike-out application, Court of Appeal hearing, and ECJ reference up to amendment.
enrichment.ratio: Where strike-out proceedings succeed on the pleaded Regulation-based claim but the claimants survive only by amending on an unpleaded Article 10 basis identified by the ECJ, the defendants are the successful party for costs of the issues actually fought.
legal_issues: Whether defendants should recover costs of strike-out, appeal, and ECJ reference
Whether the Article 10 amendment changed the costs outcome
Whether legal aid assessment should apply for the defended period

confidence.notes: Judgment is costs-only after substantive ECJ ruling. Underlying levy merits not re-decided here.

notes: Long-running employment directions permission application; procedural history complex but decision grounds are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Permission refused on employment tribunal directions appeal
key_facts: Dr Garg, a locum consultant psychiatrist, brought race discrimination proceedings against Wolverhampton Health Authority after employment ended on 31 December 1992.
An employment tribunal found in 1993 that his discrimination claim was in time on the basis employment ended on that date; later courts rejected his attempts to reopen that finding.
At a 2001 directions hearing Chairman Crump defined live discrimination issues, refused adjournment pending stale High Court actions, and refused two witness summonses.
The EAT dismissed Dr Garg's interlocutory appeal; he applied to the Court of Appeal for permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from an Employment Appeal Tribunal order dismissing an interlocutory appeal against employment tribunal case management directions.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no real prospect of success on any ground.
enrichment.ratio: A litigant cannot relitigate a finally determined employment termination date to pursue post-dismissal wage claims; refusal of adjournment and witness summonses where witnesses related to an irrelevant continued-employment issue was a proper exercise of discretion; there is no general right to publicly funded counsel in employment discrimination proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the employment termination date could be reopened
Whether refusal of adjournment pending High Court proceedings was wrong
Whether refusal of witness summonses was a misuse of discretion
Whether Dr Garg's human rights were breached by lack of legal representation
Whether EAT procedure was unfair

confidence.notes: Permission decision and procedural points are explicit. Substantive discrimination merits remain undetermined.

notes: Typical Nepal asylum permission application dismissed as abusive; very short judgment with clear outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum judicial review permission appeal dismissed as abusive
key_facts: Mr Gurung's asylum claim was refused by the Secretary of State and dismissed on appeal by an adjudicator who found him untruthful and unreliable.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal on credibility grounds.
Richards J refused judicial review on paper; Lindsay J refused renewed permission when the applicant did not attend.
The applicant sought permission to appeal with generic grounds about documentary evidence, law, and country conditions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against refusal of permission to apply for judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed as an abuse of process and totally without merit.
enrichment.ratio: Generic formulae that documentary evidence, relevant law, and country conditions were not considered are not proper grounds of appeal where the adjudicator's adverse credibility findings provide a sound basis for refusal and successive courts have already rejected the claim.
legal_issues: Whether the Immigration Appeal Tribunal erred in refusing permission to appeal
Whether judicial review grounds disclosed an arguable error of law
Whether generic Nepal asylum appeal grounds are sufficient

confidence.notes: Very short procedural judgment with unambiguous dismissal. No detailed country guidance analysis.

notes: Contributory negligence apportionment permission refusal; Froom v Butcher distinction clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Contributory negligence apportionment in drunk pedestrian road accident
key_facts: Mr Parkinson sustained severe injuries when he walked past a parked taxi into the path of a Dyfed Powys Police car on 28 February 1998.
He was intoxicated; the police officer drove at 40 mph in a built-up area late at night.
The judge found both parties negligent and apportioned liability 65% to the defendant and 35% to the claimant.
Expert evidence indicated secondary serious injuries would have been avoided at a proper speed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against contributory negligence apportionment in a county court road traffic claim.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; judge's 65/35 apportionment not open to interference.
enrichment.ratio: Apportionment of responsibility between a negligent driver and an intoxicated pedestrian is not analogous to seat-belt contributory negligence under Froom v Butcher because the driver of a car owes duties to others as to speed and care, and where excessive speed causatively increased the severity of injury the driver's fault may properly attract the greater share of liability.
legal_issues: Whether 65% liability on the police driver was clearly wrong
Whether Froom v Butcher seat-belt principles apply to intoxicated pedestrian cases
Relative causative potency of driver speed versus claimant intoxication

confidence.notes: Apportionment reasoning and refusal of permission are explicit.

notes: Misrepresentation and qualified privilege defamation retrial; Horrocks v Lowe malice analysis thoroughly reviewed.

enrichment.short_title: Misrepresentation and privileged defamation claims dismissed on retrial
key_facts: Mr Orford sued Rasmi Electronics and its managing director for misrepresentation and defamation arising from his 1999 employment as an electronic development manager.
He claimed he was not told he would have to copy competitors' products unlawfully; the defendants' HSE report stated he fabricated a workplace accident.
After a successful first appeal, a retrial before HHJ Walton dismissed both claims and ordered Orford to pay 75% of defendants' costs.
Orford later succeeded in a separate personal injury claim establishing the accident occurred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal with extension of time against dismissal of misrepresentation/deceit and defamation claims after retrial.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no real prospect of overturning factual findings on misrepresentation or qualified privilege/malice.
enrichment.ratio: Silence at interview about possible reverse engineering does not amount to actionable misrepresentation where agreed terms concerned quality and cost without time pressure; a defamatory HSE report published on qualified privilege is protected unless express malice is proved, and careless or over-eager forensic conduct does not establish reckless or dishonest belief under Horrocks v Lowe.
legal_issues: Whether interview silence amounted to misrepresentation inducing employment
Whether copying instructions were unlawful
Whether defendants honestly believed the accident was fabricated
Whether qualified privilege was defeated by malice
Whether the 75% costs order was wrong

confidence.notes: Detailed permission judgment on fact-heavy defamation and misrepresentation issues. Personal injury outcome noted but not appealed.

notes: Standard Nepal asylum permission application; procedural delay and lack of point of law clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum judicial review permission appeal dismissed for delay
key_facts: Mr Rana, a Nepalese national refused leave to enter in October 2001, failed before an immigration adjudicator in May 2002.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal in July 2002, but judicial review was not sought until September 2003.
McCombe J and Davis J refused permission to apply for judicial review; the applicant did not attend before Davis J.
He appealed out of time with generic grounds and sought to rely on new country information.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against refusal of permission to apply for judicial review of an immigration adjudicator's asylum decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no arguable point of law and excessive delay.
enrichment.ratio: Judicial review and Court of Appeal appeals in asylum cases require identifiable errors of law, not fresh country evidence or boilerplate complaints that documents, law, and country information were ignored; long unexplained delay is fatal to permission.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review was out of time
Whether any point of law arose from the adjudicator's decision
Whether new country evidence could be raised on appeal
Whether generic grounds stated a proper appeal

confidence.notes: Procedural dismissal with clear reasoning. No substantive asylum merits decided.
